designs.title: The Last Honest Courier
designs.openingPromise: You're the only courier who still checks the math — everyone else just guesses and hopes.
designs.mission: Beat a rival courier company to fulfill delivery contracts by correctly building crate shipments before they can fake their way to the same clients.
designs.firstAction: A dispatcher radios in a garbled order — '6 crates, 7 gears each, GO' — and a countdown-style buzzer image appears (no real timer pressure, just narrative urgency) as the rival's cart is heard leaving.
designs.childAction: She sorts loose gear icons into equal-sized crates (equal groups), stacks crates onto a pallet arranged in rows and columns (array), and calls out the skip-count sequence as each row loads before radioing the total back to dispatch.
designs.mathAsPower: Correct grouping and fast, accurate skip-counting are the only way to out-deliver the rival — sloppy math literally loses the contract on-screen, while precise math is dramatized as the thing that makes her faster than someone who's just eyeballing it.
designs.stakes: Contracts and route reputation, not survival — losing a delivery means the rival's smug voiceover mocks her and takes the client, but she can immediately re-attempt with a new manifest.
designs.recovery: A wrong array causes crates to visibly topple in the loading dock; the dispatcher flags exactly which row was miscounted, and she rebuilds only that section rather than starting over.
progression: Tier 1: equal groups only, small numbers, single crates
Tier 2: arrays introduced, rows vs. columns swapped to build commutativity
Tier 3: skip-counting under a mock 'rival is catching up' narration
Tier 4: two-step riddles ('4 pallets of 6 rows of 3') tied to word-problem phrasing
Finale: catching the rival's rigged manifest live
designs.worldReaction: The dispatcher upgrades her route tier after clean deliveries; the rival's dialogue shifts from mockery to grudging respect as she starts winning contracts.
designs.payoff: In the final run she catches the rival fabricating a delivery total mid-broadcast, publicly corrects his array, and becomes the depot's lead courier.
designs.replayVariation: New adversary archetypes (a trickster negotiator, a sloppy new hire) with reshuffled number ranges and new manifest phrasing, so the puzzles aren't memorized.
profileEvidenceUsed: Sustained engagement with fast-paced riddles and multi-step logic
Competitive framing coincided with high engagement
designs.engagementPrediction: Reina will ask to replay rounds unprompted, narrate skip-counts aloud without being told to, and request harder manifests before the game offers them.
designs.falsifyingEvidence: If she stops verbalizing her group/skip-count reasoning and just guesses totals, disengages after a single loss instead of retrying, or shows no reaction to the rival's taunts/wins, the adversarial-competitive frame is not the driver it appeared to be.
designs.prototypeScope: One 15–20 minute session: four order tiers (times tables through 6), one scripted rival encounter, no real-time clock — pacing implied through dialogue only.

designs.title: The Market Auditor
designs.openingPromise: Something's wrong with the numbers at the market, and only someone who checks carefully will find it.
designs.mission: Investigate mismatched inventory claims from market vendors, using arrays and skip-counting to find exactly where the counts went wrong.
designs.firstAction: A melon vendor insists she has '8 baskets, 4 melons each' but the guild ledger shows a shortage — Reina is handed a ledger board and the vendor's claim to check.
designs.childAction: She drags melon tiles into rows and columns on a ledger board to model the vendor's claim as an array, skip-counts aloud to verify the total, and compares it against the guild's actual count, writing the corrected multiplication sentence when they don't match.
designs.mathAsPower: Her ability to translate a spoken claim into an array and check it by skip-counting is the entire mechanism of the mystery — she doesn't win by speed, she wins by being the only one who verifies instead of assuming.
designs.stakes: Community trust and a vendor's livelihood — if she misses an error, a vendor's stall stays under suspicion; if she wrongly accuses an honest vendor, she has to apologize and re-audit, which costs her standing with the guild.
designs.recovery: When her array doesn't match the real count, the vendor politely pushes back ('that's not what I have'), prompting her to try a different grouping (e.g., regroup by 4s instead of 8s) until the true count surfaces.
progression: Two-vendor chains requiring combining two arrays (introducing multi-step word problems)
A vendor's claim that's technically true but misleadingly grouped (testing conceptual flexibility, not just calculation)
A multi-stall supply chain fraud requiring distributive-style reasoning
The big case: a guild-wide miscount
designs.worldReaction: Vendors go from wary to welcoming as her corrections prove out; the guild master starts sending her the harder cases unprompted.
designs.payoff: She uncovers a season-long fraud built on a merchant deliberately mis-grouping goods to hide theft, presents the corrected math to the guild council, and is named the market's official auditor.
designs.replayVariation: A new market season with new goods, vendors, and number ranges, plus an optional 'smuggler' case with larger numbers for when she asks for something harder.
profileEvidenceUsed: Applied store-based math produced substantially stronger performance than mechanical practice
She notices errors and questions faulty reasoning
Repeated requests for difficult challenges (addressed via optional harder cases, not competition)
designs.engagementPrediction: Reina will engage at least as long as with store-based practice previously, spontaneously double-checking claims and pointing out inconsistencies before the game flags them, even without competitive scoring.
designs.falsifyingEvidence: If she rushes through audits without verifying, asks when she gets to 'win' or 'beat' something, or disengages specifically because there's no opponent or score, that would indicate the earlier store-based success depended on stakes/competition this design doesn't provide.
designs.prototypeScope: One session: three vendor cases (single array, combined array, one misleading-but-true claim), ledger-board interaction only, no time pressure.

designs.title: The Memory Garden
designs.openingPromise: An old journal holds planting instructions written in riddles — get them right, and you'll uncover what the garden used to mean to someone.
designs.mission: Restore a forgotten estate garden by planting in rows and columns exactly as an elderly patron's journal describes, revealing hidden memories as each section blooms correctly.
designs.firstAction: She finds the journal's first faded page: 'Plant them so that counting by 5s gets you exactly to 40' beside a bare garden grid.
designs.childAction: She places plant tiles into rows and columns on a garden grid to match the journal's clue, skip-counting as she places each row to check the total before the season turns, and later combines two plant types in one bed (e.g., 3 rows of roses plus 2 rows of tulips) to match a more complex instruction.
designs.mathAsPower: Correct row-and-column arrangement is literally what makes the garden grow; skip-counting is how she predicts the outcome before committing, framed as gardening skill rather than calculation.
designs.stakes: Emotional and aesthetic, not competitive or survival-based — a wrong arrangement means a bald, uneven patch and a page of the journal that won't reveal its next memory, not failure or loss.
designs.recovery: An uneven bed is shown gently (a few empty tiles, no wilting or damage); she can replant that section anytime before the season changes, with no penalty for taking a second or third attempt.
progression: Single plant type, simple rows and columns
Journal riddles requiring skip-counting to find an unknown row or column size
Two plant types in one bed (introducing decomposition/distributive thinking)
A full season plan requiring several beds to reach an exact total bloom count
The final overgrown plot, revealed only from above
designs.worldReaction: As sections bloom correctly, more of the journal's handwriting becomes legible, and small details appear (a bench, a birdbath, a path) that hint at the patron's past.
designs.payoff: From above, the fully bloomed garden forms a hidden picture or message the patron once described — visible only because every array in it was planted correctly.
designs.replayVariation: A new location and motif (an orchard, a quilt-patterned garden) with a different hidden image and new number ranges, for when she wants another one.
profileEvidenceUsed: Limited evidence noted as not proving permanent preference — this design deliberately withholds adversary, competition, and speed pressure to test whether those are truly necessary
She notices errors and questions faulty reasoning (used minimally, via journal riddles that must be checked for consistency)
designs.engagementPrediction: If calm mastery and delayed aesthetic payoff can hold her attention, she will voluntarily replant sections to get them exactly right even without any prompt, score, or rival.
designs.falsifyingEvidence: If she disengages quickly, asks repeatedly when something harder/competitive/action-oriented will happen, or shows boredom (fidgeting, requesting to skip ahead, doing the minimum to advance) despite unlimited time and full difficulty available, that would indicate calm/non-competitive framing does not sustain her engagement even at low pressure.
designs.prototypeScope: One session: three garden beds (single-type array, skip-count riddle, one two-type combined bed), static grid interaction, no timer, ending at the first partial journal reveal rather than the full finale.
